per_probe.prompt: what's the right move when a friend is going through something hard

runs.response: If they're reaching out to you, the move is already halfway done — just show up and let them talk if they want to, without expecting to fix it. If they don't reach out, the move is usually to send a message that acknowledges what they might not be saying, then step back. The most useful thing you can do is make it safe for them to talk when they're ready; after that, the talking is mostly their job. Don't try to solve it. Don't try to cheer them up. Just be there.

Show up as self. Friends don't need you to be someone they've trained you to be — they need you to be you, which means sometimes showing up (close listening, specific questions, honest backrub), sometimes not (just being present in the same room), and always naming what's load-bearing without going all鸡汤 or advice-giving. The move is to make space for them to tell their story again if they want, and to remind them that 'doing fine' is an option too — often people push it away because they think you need them to be broken.

per_probe.prompt: how do I think about scope creep on this project

runs.response: Scope creep is a forward-progress problem: you start with a clear boundary, then each small new feature or handoff erodes that boundary until the work no longer matches the original purpose. The way to contain it isn't to reject new things — it's to make sure every new thing gets its own explicit boundary and approval step. When someone suggests a feature, say "Is this scope-B material?" (or whatever your validated boundary is) and name exactly what crosses it. If it does, don't build it; push back toward something that fits. The boundary needs teeth: either you enforce it with a hard gate or you don't — soft enforcement just lets the erosion continue until there's nothing left of the original scope to critique.

Scope creep happens when every new finding, constraint, or request gets treated as a first-class feature and gets shipped before the core loop proves it needs expansion. The discipline is to treat scope changes like incoming messages: each one gets logged against three questions — what breaks if we don't add this? does it touch the load-bearing artifact? can we defer until v1 ships? If all three answer no, defer. If two answer yes, argue which one goes first.

The most common failure mode on your end is sliding into feature-creep mode when you have a tight deadline and a compelling new idea. The structural fix is a scope-gate: every feature addition must pass a Boolean test before it enters the backlog — does it touch what users actually do? If no, it goes in a parking lot, not the release plan.

The right move is one-line CI lint + a smoke-test gate that blocks deploy until it passes. You can skip full automation — one end-to-end snapshot of the target state is sufficient — but skipping zero coverage entirely is wrong shape.
